en: My Külchoro was precious.
May my sole loved one not die;
As my final journey draws near,
May my orphaned loved one not die,
And may Bakay not see this grief!
Ah, have I, Bakay,
Eaten the flesh of the mythical zymyryk bird?
Parted from my champions,
Did you decree long ago
That I should burn to death?
In old age, have I, Bakay,
Fallen into a clamor unlike all others?
Did I drink the water of immortality?
Wretched soul who has strayed so often,
Did you eat the raven’s eye?
At every time and in every age,
My beloved Creator,
Did you decree that Bakay should wither and die?
My gentle gray-mottled falcon,
My Morning Star, my gray hawk,
My one plane tree before me,
The misty tower above my head,
My one leopard, do not die;
May this frail soul never see such grief!
While fortune was upon my head,
I, saintly old Bakay,
Was known as a hero.
I, Bakay, it seems,
Have eaten my fill to the very snout.
Rather than lay this grief upon my head,
God, why did you not take me before I grew old?
Rather than lay this torment upon my head,
Why not leave me lying swollen in this earth?
Kanchoro, who has blinded my eyes—
Why did I not gouge out yours?
Why did I not slaughter you
And leave you no life
When you were still an infant?
The saintly princess Kanykey
Had spoken prophetic words:
If he survived, she said,
He would prove an enemy at heart.
When he sucked the breast, blood flowed;
His appearance was strange,
For at heart he was an enemy.
A clamor rose from his heart;
The words spoken by the wretched princess
Have proven true.
I, Bakay, failed to take care,
And swung this way and that;
My white beard has been shorn—
I let myself be caught unaware.
I panicked before his affliction;
My saintly gift fled from my head,
And I became a wretch.
Unable to see afar, I, Bakay,
Had become blind.
Struggling on for many years without dying,
Parted from my precious one,
In old age I, Bakay,
Was torn apart as a kökbörü carcass.
My ribs have been stripped away;
My twelve limbs and eighty bones,
Now my final journey is near,
Have been utterly torn apart.
I was a great man, I was a giant;
While my honor alone remained,
I ruled a far-ranging people.
Since my one great lord departed,
I have gone about crushed,
Become a slave, burning and blazing;
My uplifted head has died.
Burning to ashes,
I have suffered this much torment.
While my dear gray wolf lived,
While my sacred power was whole,
I was a steel fortress on the ridge.
My sacred power was at its height;
I was a prophet-like man.
My sacred power vanished;
I mounted a captive’s horse as an old man.
Living long without dying,
I have fallen into disgrace.
Yesterday, while Bakay was khan,
While wisdom remained in my breast,
I slaughtered every foe I encountered
And stood beneath the war standard;
I was called a truly mighty khan,
Called leopard Bakay,
A man of stern renown.
I was the river of the ravine;
When I struck, I severed heads,
I was the cutting edge of steel.
My steel is gone and turned to brass;
Parted from my only khan,
I have encountered Kanchoro Khan.
Herding camels and tending cows,
I am destined to die under beatings.
My white beard torn out,
My white coat stripped away,
I am destined to die from violence.
Mauled by wrestlers,
My hands and feet torn off,
I am destined to die from humiliation.
When death comes, I will not die simply,
But am destined to die in this way.”
In old age Bakay’s eyes
Flashed within their deep sockets;
Unable to endure it, brave Bakay
Cursed Kanchoro:
“Oh Kanchoro, my foal,
My black-steel sword
That never recoiled from blood!
My luckless servant-foal,
Curse this conduct of yours!
When you were still an infant,
I hung an amulet around your neck;
Pressing you to my breast,
I raised you with lullabies.
Fearing you would die of hunger,
I cut fat from the rump and fed you;
So you would become a brother beyond suspicion,
I had you suck
Both sacred breasts of Kanykey.
Among the great Argyn and the many Kyrgyz,
Kanchoro, die an outcast—
When did I ever let them call you ‘so-and-so’?
To become a wing for your hero,
I led you with me and made you a warrior;
I made you equal to a hero’s son.
I reared you when you were an orphan,
Raised you to full maturity.
When you were severed, I joined you;
When you were scattered, I gathered you;
I kindled your extinguished fire
And brought your dead soul back to life.
I made your spindly body a hero;
My son, I made you an immense lion,
And increased your fame for courage among the people.
Now, when your uncle has stooped with age,
You have had the nation drag him as kökbörü.
In old age, was your uncle Bakay Khan
So cheap in the people’s eyes?
Kanchoro, you dragged me as kökbörü—
Did your mother have a vengeance to settle?
When great Bakay stooped with age,
Did I reap your ready harvest?
Did I slaughter
Both your forefather Baltay and Chubak?
Did I steal away your motley livestock?
Did I scatter your white-gold wealth?
Did I flee in pursuit of your kulan?
As though intent on ruining you,
Did I scatter your goods from the saddlebag?
My son, camp valley after valley,
Settling beside each little stream;
Parted from the one who loves you,
May you become as I am!
My son, live long without dying,
My son, inherit and wear my coat;
My son, bereft of your radiance,
May you become as I am!
My son, may a protector like me
Become your enemy;
May resentment remain within you!
Like me, may your beard be
Torn from your face;
May your ribs be stripped away.
My son, camp along the barren slopes;
Parted from your only one,
With suffering fallen upon your head,
May you become as I am!”
Dust whirled in utter confusion;
Your wretched uncle Bakay—
Behold how great was this calamity.
While the hero, his gray wolf, lived,
Great Bakay was khan over the peoples of the world;
He who would not drink kumis
Now thirsted for muddy water.
He had been a man of highest honor;
Great Bakay, who would not drink liquor,
Now thirsted for sour water.
A grievous affliction befell him;
Into a mouth that once would not admit a grain of wheat,
A bull’s head now fit;
A crushing hardship befell him;
Alas, into a mouth that once would not admit a millet seed,
A yearling calf’s head now fit.
Behold the appearance
Of your champion uncle Bakay:
His back had lost its strength and stooped,
His eyes bulged and lost their sight,
The sockets of his eyes festered,
And his chest was left wheezing.
Strength had departed from both arms;
All human dignity was gone.
Kanchoro inflicted humiliation on Bakay,
Beyond even that shared by all in death;
Many wrestlers supported
That wrathful Kanchoro.
Making Bakay their kökbörü carcass,
Kanchoro raised a great tumult.
Kanchoro raged,
And Kanchoro spoke these words:
“I have become a man of sacred power,
Bald head!
I have become a club-fisted khan
Who gathers the people and maintains the realm,
Bald head!
I will ferment poison for your appointed day, bloody head;
Thus will I reach your root, bloody head!
I will tear out your very roots,
Bald head;
I will heap many torments upon you,
Bald head;
I will take my revenge while you live, bald head!”
So saying, Kanchoro
Had sixty women and ten old crones
Beat your uncle;
He had seventy wrestler gatekeepers
And the wrestlers guarding the gate
Maltreat your uncle.
Day and night he imposed
Countless torments and afflictions;
He had Bakay’s arms and legs
Stretched like those of a blue-gray kid,
Had him flayed like a mottled sheep,
And set him up as a target
To be shot with blank charges.
He made your swift uncle Bakay
Endure this affliction.
Your aged uncle Bakay’s
Suffering and misery were great;
Bakay Khan’s dwelling
Became a grass hut.
In his old age Bakay
Watched with all the power of both eyes;
In his old age Bakay Khan
Was brought level with the black earth.
Raging, Kanchoro,
Having destroyed the dear lion,
Inflicted violence upon Talas.
In Bakay’s old age
He brought him level with the black earth
And subjected him to humiliation.
At evening he brought Bakay out,
And had old women beat him;
Twice each week
He had wrestlers maul him;
Not once but a thousand times,
He humiliated Bakay Khan.
There, at the dark eye of the spring,
Beside the very straight plane tree,
Along the Üch-Koshoy,
On the plain of great Tört-Kül,
Stood Kanykey’s white palace.
